stories.title: US envoys Witkoff, Kushner in Moscow for peace talks
stories.summary: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who were sent by US President Donald Trump with a new peace plan for the Ukraine war, have arrived in Moscow for talks. The move marks Washington's latest bid to break a diplomatic stalemate in Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. US outlet Axios reported they would meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow today, and then Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv tomorrow. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev will meet Mr Witkoff and Mr Kushner upon their arrival in Moscow, two people familiar with the upcoming visit said. Mr Dmitriev, who told Reuters in June that he had remained in contact with the US negotiators during a pause in their visits to Russia, took part in all their previous meetings with Mr Putin. He also played a role in negotiating US sanction waivers for Russian oil this year.

stories.title: Domestic economy sees 3.1% growth in first half of 2026
stories.summary: The domestic economy grew by a healthy 3.1% in the first six months of this year, according to the latest figures from the Central Statistics Office. The strong performance was driven by personal spending which was up 2.8% in the first half of 2026. Today's figures mean the economy is in a strong position ahead of the Budget which will be announced on October 6. However, the CSO figures show volatile output by multinationals resulted in a 7% fall in Gross Domestic Product (GDP) – the measure of the economy which includes the impact of foreign companies - in the first six months. The multinational dominated sectors of the economy fell by 11.5%. This was mainly caused by a surge in pharmaceutical exports in March 2025 which was not repeated this year and consequently resulted in an overall fall in output by multinationals this year.

stories.title: Under-18 e-scooter ban could be in place by end of month
stories.summary:
Minister for Transport Darragh O'Brien has said a ban on the use of e-scooters by under 18s could now be introduced by the end of this month or early next month, after he received permission from Europe to proceed with the plans. The State had been advised that it needed to wait three months before the ban could be introduced, due to European rules, but Minister O'Brien received confirmation this afternoon that the European Commission had waived this waiting period, after accepting the case to have an urgent adoption of the measures. Minister O'Brien has welcomed the decision, saying he will now move to draft the necessary regulations, with a view to increasing the minimum age for e-scooter use from 16 to 18 by late September or early October.

Regulations to make helmets and high-visibility clothing mandatory for e-scooter use come into effect from tomorrow. Those in breach of the regulations face a fixed charge notice of €100. From 2 October fees for detention and storage of seized e-scooters will be doubled, rising to €80 for detention and the first day of storage and €30 for each additional day or storage. In the coming weeks fixed Charge Notices will be increased to €100 for e-scooter offences.

stories.title: Can the EU find its energy independence in the Arctic?
stories.summary: Shrouded in darkness for six months of the year and sparsely populated, the Arctic's vast expanse may appear too remote to rank high on the EU's agenda. Yet, Brussels's focus on the High North has sharpened in recent years for security and economic reasons. The melting Arctic ice caps have opened up tempting yet controversial opportunities for drilling and mining. This year, the EU is set to revise its Arctic strategy and decide what it actually wants from the region. The Arctic had long been seen as a model of international collaboration despite wider geopolitical tensions. The Arctic nations – Russia, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Canada and the US – have worked together on issues ranging from climate change and shipping to fisheries and security.

stories.title: Nigel Farage defends himself over foreign donation claims
stories.summary: Nigel Farage has sought to defend himself over allegations Reform had broken laws on political donations as he addressed his party conference. In a speech delayed by a "security alert" and interrupted four times by hecklers, Mr Farage vowed not to be "distracted" from his agenda by what he called a "highly co-ordinated campaign of attacks". The annual gathering at Birmingham's NEC has been overshadowed by yet more allegations about party funding after Channel 4 broadcast footage that appeared to show senior Reform figures discussing how to disguise donations from foreign donors. The footage was part of an investigation by undercover group Verbatim, who posed as an American donor and his son who had paid for polling allegedly commissioned by Reform and were seeking to channel money to Reform. Accepting donations from a foreign company, including donations in kind such as polling, could constitute a criminal offence, and the party has been reported to the police. The Liberal Democrats have also asked Parliament's standards watchdog to investigate the claims.

stories.title: Joyce exit brings down curtain on colourful era
stories.summary: Padraic Joyce's departure brings to an end a colourful and tumultuous era in Galway football. A vibrant presence in the managerial paddock has exited stage left. Those pristine white runners will no longer traipse the inter-county sideline. The airpods have gone back in the case. The media will miss his occasionally unpredictable bluntness and his penchant for issuing cutting verdicts on his star players' performances. Rumours had swirled around social media in the week leading up to the All-Ireland final that Joyce was about to quit. On this desk, inquiries were made about whether we needed to have a 'Joyce departs...' article prepared and ready to go. Public denials were issued. There were, it has to be said, plenty of Galway supporters who wanted him gone in the wake of their sickening quarter-final defeat to Dublin. From our own sampling of the mood at the time, it's doubtful whether he would have survived a plebiscite within the county that week. But it appeared for all the world he was set on digging in and remaining at the helm. He was going to manage Galway to Sam or die trying.

stories.title: Knockout KO'd - Tyrone continue to go against the grain
stories.summary: Quiz question - name the two counties that still employ a straight knockout format in their senior men's football championship? You should get halfway there given the fame attached with Tyrone’s continued decision to ignore changing times - and the much-cited fact that no club has retained the title since Carrickmore all the way back in 2005. The action throws in tonight with the meeting of Ardboe and Edendork while Loughmacrory will be hoping to end that back-to-back hex when they meet Dungannon on Saturday, but the fact of the matter is that if they’re not good enough then their title defence will be over at about 9pm this evening. The other county who still employs knockout football is less obvious, probably the last footballing county to come to mind. stories.title: No away fans at Celtic v Rangers games this season
stories.summary: Celtic and Rangers fans will not be present in each other's grounds for the rest of the season. The absence of away allocations has been announced by the SPFL after Celtic challenged Rangers’ decision to give them just 300 tickets for the Premier Sports Cup tie at Ibrox on 13 September. Rangers cut the allocation from the recently-agreed total of about 2,500 seats in response to the trouble that marred the Scottish Cup quarter-final clash between the Glasgow rivals in March, when Celtic were given the traditional allocation of about 8,000 under competition rules. An SPFL statement read: "Following the events of March 8 and the publication of the Independent Review, the arrangements for the forthcoming fixtures were reconsidered. "For the Premier Sports Cup tie at Ibrox, Rangers proposed a reduced away allocation based on its assessment of the circumstances and risks associated with that fixture. Celtic did not accept that proposal and sought a determination from the SPFL. "After further discussions involving both clubs and the SPFL, agreement has been reached that there will be no away supporters for matches involving Rangers and Celtic in SPFL competitions for the remainder of the 2026/27 season.

stories.title: O'Gara poised to sign new La Rochelle deal - report
stories.summary: Ronan O'Gara looks set to end speculation about his immediate future, with reports that he's close to signing a new contract with La Rochelle. The former Munster out-half and current La Rochelle head coach has been one of the standout candidates linked with succeeding Leo Cullen at Leinster. Cullen will step down from his role with Leinster at the end of the season and the province's chief executive Shane Nolan was coy when asked about the prospect of O'Gara replacing Cullen. O'Gara himself added fuel to the speculation in his Irish Examiner column last week. "The way some blue boys speak of you suggests I should be searching in my greying roots for devil horns in the morning," O'Gara wrote. "The Ronan O'Gara those lads remember from 20 years ago is not the coach of today, or indeed anything like him." In the same column he revealed that he had started conversations with La Rochelle about a contract extension, and now French sports outlet Midi Olympique is reporting the O'Gara is poised to sign a new four-year deal.

stories.title: Something for the Weekend: Pauline Scanlon's cultural picks
stories.summary: Pauline Scanlon is one of Ireland's most distinctive voices, an artist deeply rooted in tradition yet constantly pushing its boundaries. A West Kerry native, her singing carries the weight of old songs while speaking powerfully to the present day. From her acclaimed debut Red Colour Sun to her work with LUMIERE, John Spillane, Dónal Lunny Damien Dempsey, Sinéad O’Connor and The Whileaways, Scanlon has built a career of remarkable collaborations and solo performances. She's recently been named TG4 Singer of the Year, to be presented at the Gradam Ceoil Awards in Limerick on September 13th. Gaza, directed by Garry Keane and Andrew McConnell. I've seen Gaza numerous times over the last number of years, often at Palestinian events, and it sears through to the heart every single time. What I find so powerful about the film is its refusal to offer a reductive portrayal of life in Gaza. Instead, it shows us its complexity: the humour, music, family, work, love, frustration, beauty and ordinary human ambition that exist alongside the brutality of life under blockade. As it was first released in 2019, watching it now carries an almost unbearable weight, but that insistence on the fullness and complexity of life is what makes the film so beautiful and affecting. I’ve had two records on repeat this summer. Child Ballads by Anaïs Mitchell and Jefferson Hamer is a collection of songs I love, sung with the most exquisite harmonies. There is a simplicity and intimacy to the whole record that really draws me in, and I’ve found myself returning to it again and again. The other is An Sionnach Dubh by Dàibhidh Stiùbhard from Co. Tyrone. Dàibhidh is, for me, one of the most beautiful traditional singers of his generation. He is such an accomplished singer, with a gorgeous repertoire and a real depth to his singing. As someone who loves traditional song, it is always exciting to hear a singer with that combination of ability, sensitivity and a great store of songs.

stories.title: Electric Picnic 2027 sells out before line-up announced
stories.summary: Electric Picnic 2027 has sold out after tickets for next year's festival went on sale on Friday morning. Organisers confirmed that tickets, which went on sale at 10am through the festival’s loyalty scheme and general sale, have now been snapped up. No acts have yet been announced for the 2027 festival, which will take place at Stradbally Hall in Co Laois from Friday 27 to Sunday 29 August. stories.title: Conor Pope's tips for saving money at home this winter
stories.summary: "Generally speaking, winter is very expensive," says Pope, explaining that heating and lighting our homes in the colder, darker months adds up. Additionally, the need to tumble dry clothes can be a big expense, alongside buying warmer clothing, extra food, and saving up for Christmas presents. "I've done the maths, and I reckon that winter time costs about €10,000 more for the average household than summer time," he states. "That's not even being wildly extravagant." The first step in bringing those costs down? Shopping around for an electricity provider. "The reality is that more than 70% of Irish consumers don't switch their energy provider," the savvy saver explains, "despite the fact that, even in a climate of rising prices, you can still knock about €500 off your annual bill - just by moving from company A to company B." Many people will avoid switching because it feels like too much hassle, but Pope insists that sites like Bonkers.ie and Switcher.ie make it incredibly straightforward.

stories.title: State memorial 100 years after Dromcollogher cinema fire
stories.summary: A State commemoration for the 48 people who died in the Dromcollogher cinema fire takes place today, marking the centenary of one of the deadliest disasters in Irish history. Taoiseach Micheál Martin, accompanied by Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport Patrick O'Donovan, will officiate at a formal ceremony in Dromcollogher at midday to honour the victims. On 5 September 1926, around 150 people gathered in a makeshift cinema in the Co Limerick town to watch two films. A candle fell and ignited highly flammable nitrate film during the screening, causing the fire to spread rapidly through the temporary venue, which was located upstairs in a large wooden loft. A wooden ladder was the only means of entering and leaving the building. Those closest to the exit managed to escape, but many others became trapped and the intensity of the blaze made rescue efforts extremely difficult.

stories.summary: New e-scooter rules which came into force today punish responsible users, a group representing commuters has said. The regulations require e-scooter users to wear helmets and high-visibility clothing. Chair of the Dublin Commuter Coalition Jason Cullen said he does not think the regulations are the right approach. "Its major impact is going to be that compliant e-scooter users will now have another barrier to entry. We want and need better enforcement. "Since these measures were announced, we've seen an uptick in garda resourcing and 40 plus e-scooters per day around the city are being seized, the illegally used ones. "What we want is better guided resourcing and better operations for managing that anti-social behaviour and illegal behaviour in community, so that those people who are compliant can continue to use them in a safe way."

stories.summary: Minister for European Affairs Thomas Byrne has said he is "absolutely confident" that agreement can be reached on the next long-term EU budget before Ireland's Presidency of the EU concludes at the end of the year. One of the key aim's of Ireland's EU Presidency is to agree the budget, known as the multiannual financial framework (MFF), before the end of the year. However, several countries, including Germany, want to rein in spending. Speaking as he arrived at Dublin Castle for the meeting of the General Affairs Council, Mr Byrne stressed the urgency of the negotiations. "I'm absolutely confident we can achieve this by the end of the year because I think we need to, and the reason we need to is because we need to have the funds in place by the 1 January 2028.

stories.title: Volkswagen flags 50,000 more job cuts across car group
stories.summary: Volkswagen shares hit an 11-week high after the supervisory board of Europe's largest automaker last night struck an ambitious turnaround agreement that put the focus on sweeping job cuts and averted a clash between major stakeholders. The deal on the biggest restructuring in the group's 89-year history includes a further 50,000 job cuts, bringing the total agreed to 100,000, and leaves open the future of four of its German plants. Volkswagen, like most of its European peers, is under pressure from painful tariffs in the US, falling sales in former cash cow China and aggressive Asian rivals entering the stagnant European market. All these factors have gnawed at the group's operating margin, which stood at 3.8% in the first half, down from 7.9% in 2022, its peak over the past decade. Shareholders and analysts expressed relief that Volkswagen - with a workforce of more than 650,000, a complex structure and powerful stakeholder groups - is still able to make far-reaching decisions in times of crisis. Ingo Speich of Volkswagen shareholder Deka Investment called the agreement a breakthrough: "Does this mean Volkswagen is out of the woods? Definitely not. Now comes the hard part: execution."

stories.title: More than 120 dead in Yemen's worst clashes in years
stories.summary: A major offensive by Yemen's Houthis to seize control of the gateway to the Red Sea has left more than 120 people dead in the country's deadliest clashes in years, sources said. Fighting erupted after the Iran-backed Houthis launched a ground assault along with rocket and drone attacks near coastal areas, vying for control of the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait at the Red Sea's southern entrance. Yemen, embroiled in more than a decade of civil conflict, in July became the latest country to be drawn into the Middle East war as the Houthis upended a 2022 truce with the Saudi-backed government. Since then, the Houthis have imposed a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and repeatedly attacked its ships in the Red Sea -- a vital alternative route for oil exports after Iran all but halted Gulf shipments by blockading the Strait of Hormuz. The rebels are now trying to tighten their hold over the Red Sea, one of the world's busiest shipping lanes, which they have disrupted with attacks on passing vessels since the Gaza war broke out in 2023. The Houthi offensive aims to cut off the government-held port city of Mokha, under fire for weeks, and advance towards areas bordering the Bab al-Mandab, military sources said.

stories.title: McStay: New rule tweaks aimed at curbing slow attacks
stories.summary: For all the highs of the 2026 All-Ireland football championship, slow attacks and lateral play remain too prominent, according to Gaelic football's Expert Advisory Group (EAG) chairman Kevin McStay. Mayo's historic triumph at GAA HQ capped a swashbuckling season, but the EAG have proposed a series of rule tweaks in the upcoming third level Division 1 league. The EAG was installed on the recommendation of the Football Review Committee (FRC) in their final report in 2025, charged with monitoring trends within the game following the sweeping rule changes launched in late 2024. Of the proposed nine changes which will be trialled in the Ryan Cup this year, the four-point goal, prohibiting the fisted point, the sixth substitute and the backcourt pass were highlighted by the FRC, but didn’t make it as far as recommendations. Limiting the number of consecutive handpasses allowable to three and modifying the kickout rule, requiring the ball to travel just 13 metres rather than beyond the 40m arc, are some of the other standout adjustments. "Before the championship was played, we were up and running," he said. "We took our lead from the FRC and what was left over from their report, to see if there was anything interesting in it, if there was anything we could do to further improve it.

stories.title: Chelsea face French opposition in Champions League
stories.summary: Chelsea will play Paris Saint-Germain, Lyon, Roma, Hacken, Austria Vienna and OH Leuven in the 2026/27 Women's Champions League league phase. Katie McCabe’s side, who secured qualification with a 6-2 aggregate win over Real Sociedad, learned their fate in Friday’s draw in Nyon. The Blues will play three matches at Plough Lane and three away from home as they bid to reach the knockout stages. Arsenal have been handed a difficult draw as they face both of last year's finalists: Barcelona, who they beat in the 2024-25 final, and OL Lyonnes. Benfica, Inter Milan and Danish side HB Koga - who have Republic of Ireland international Kyra Carusa in their ranks - were also drawn to face Renée Slegers' side. Manchester City meanwhile will take on Paris St-Germain, Bayern Munich, Real Madrid, Hacken, Austria Wien and Italian side Inter Milan.

stories.summary: New Zealand have made three changes for the third test against South Africa at Soccer City on ⁠Saturday, including dropping experienced hooker Codie Taylor. Asafo Aumua will start at hooker with Samisoni Taukei'aho coming onto the bench in the change to the front row as Taylor, with 111 test caps, is left out. Sam Darry will play his first test of the four-match series as he replaces Fabian Holland in the second ‌row, with Holland dropping ⁠to the bench and Patrick Tuipulotu falling out of the matchday squad. The third change is in the backrow, where flanker Peter Lakai gets the nod over Simon Parker, with Wallace Sititi included among the replacements for the first time in ‌the test series. The backline remains unchanged from last Saturday’s 33-26 loss to the Springboks ⁠in the second test in Cape Town. The series is tied at 1-1 with the All Blacks coasting to a 33-16 victory at Ellis Park before the hosts bounced back a week later with a much-improved display.

stories.title: A House In Winter by Emily Hourican - read an extract
stories.summary: We present an extract from A House in Winter, the new novel from Emily Hourican. Set in January 1965, A House in Winter tells the story of the visit of Princess Margaret and Lord Snowden to his sister's home in Abbeyleix, Ireland, when they faced local opposition and IRA petrol bomb attacks that confined them, without electricity, for 48 fraught hours. As well as the conflict outside the walls, there's plenty within, with Margaret's difficult mother in law gleefully contributing to her disintegrating marriage. Meanwhile in the nearby village local woman Cait has struggles of her own, unable to escape family responsibilities and small town life. Both Margaret and Cait are trapped by their circumstances... 'Here, Your Highness, here!' they call, holding up cameras like babies to be admired. ‘This way!’ M rolls the window down as the car slows and the gates are opened, pulled apart by two men in cloth caps. She leans out to wave graciously. Beside her, Tony sighs. ‘I wish you wouldn’t,’ he says. ‘You’ll ruin this place. Corrupt it so that it becomes just like England – a nation of eager corgis waiting for the royal whistle.’ He laughs at his own joke, his lips parting in that toothy smile that makes him look by turns boy and wolf.

stories.title: Can stress really give you 'cortisol face'?
stories.summary: Social media is rife with discourse about 'cortisol face' and how to prevent it, but is it an actual medical complaint? Listen back to the full interview above. If you wake up with a puffy face, tired eyes and dull skin, you might have had a bad night's sleep. Or, if certain social media creators are to be believed, you're suffering from 'cortisol face'. The thoroughly online argument goes that consistent stress or burnout can lead to physical changes to your face and belly, including puffiness, swelling and rounded cheeks. However, Prof. Annie Curtis, Royal College of Surgeons of Ireland, joined Drivetime to debunk this beauty myth. "There's no such thing as cortisol face, it’s not a medical term. It’s absolutely rubbish, sorry about that." Cortisol, she explains, is one of many hormones created in the body, which act as "packages of information that are sent out from your glands to give information all around the body".

stories.title: Three killed, 23 injured in Israeli strikes on Lebanon
stories.summary: Israeli strikes in southern and eastern Lebanon have killed at least three people and injured 23, the Lebanese health ministry said. The ministry said in a statement that strikes hit five locations in the southern Tyr and Nabatieh regions and the Bekaa region in the east. It updated an earlier toll given by Lebanese official media which had reported two of the deaths in the south. The strikes came despite a truce between Israel and the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group. Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) reported the strike hit near the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge, which the Israeli army said it had captured, but Hezbollah did not confirm losing it. NNA said two young men were targeted while riding a motorcycle in the city of Nabatieh, adding that rescuers transported their bodies to a local hospital.

stories.title: Irish property prices overvalued by 17%, ESRI finds
stories.summary: Irish property prices are 17% overvalued, a new report from the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) has found. The organisation measured house prices against a range of economic fundamentals including incomes, interest rates and demographics. The ESRI said while there was "a significant degree of overvaluation" it added it was "materially lower, and structurally different in nature, than the levels observed prior to the global financial crisis". It said the current situation represented an increase in the level of overvaluation since the most recent analysis using similar methods, which was published by the ESRI in December 2024. The ESRI added: "Unlike the pre-crisis period, which was driven by excessive credit growth and loose lending standards, the current episode of overvaluation appears to be primarily an affordability issue." It said house prices have risen faster than incomes, mortgage rates have increased, and not enough homes were being built to meet demand.

stories.title: Labour proposes monthly groceries supplement at think-in
stories.summary: The Labour Party is proposing a €100-per-child monthly groceries supplement for families over the winter to help deal with the cost of living. Labour Finance Spokesperson Ged Nash put forward the proposal at the party's annual think-in Galway, the first of the autumn series of political party autumn gatherings ahead of the Dáil's return from its summer recess. Deputy Nash said the payment could constitute a €100 supplement to child benefit for families for each of their eligible offspring for three consecutive months over the winter period. "These are the kind of innovations we need. The situation is so dire for working families ... if people though the situation around groceries prices over the last two or three years was difficult, they ain't seen nothing yet once we hit January," said the Louth TD ahead of the meeting. "We are facing into a very difficult winter and this is going to be a winter dominated by the energy crisis and the need to support people with energy bills", he said. "This should not be viewed in isolation of other measures we will be announcing in our alternative budget."

stories.title: Oil heads for weekly gain as US-Iran fighting resumes
stories.summary: Oil prices were on course to gain more than 6% for the week as the US and Iran resumed military exchanges in the seventh month of their conflict, while US diesel prices hit a record high. Brent crude futures were up 6.1% for the week and US West Texas Intermediate crude futures had gained 8.3%. On the day Brent was flat at $95.54 a barrel by early evening, while WTI was down 0.6%, at $90.78. The rally in oil prices combined with a much steeper increase in fuel prices has pushed inflation and government borrowing costs higher around the world and intensified warnings that the global economy might be heading for a hard landing. "All sectors of the economy are affected by diesel. This is one of the reasons why the government bond yields in the US are so high, it's the expectation that inflation will continue to go up," said Claudio Galimberti, chief economist at Rystad Energy. Average US diesel prices hit record highs as renewed US-Iran hostilities and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries increased supply disruptions.

stories.title: Two trapped tunnel workers rescued in Nepal 'miracle'
stories.summary: Two hydropower workers have been pulled alive from a tunnel buried by debris in Nepal, a rare ray of hope on the tenth day of rescue efforts after catastrophic Himalayan flooding. Chinese state media reported 31 people killed in Tibet and 541 missing, taking the total toll from the 26 August glacial and mountain collapse to 1,318 dead and 5,624 missing. Rescuers cheered as one man emerged through a muddy opening, a video released by the energy ministry showed. He was helped to his feet by rescuers, and later carried on the backs of the emergency workers, raising his hand as they took him towards a helicopter. A photograph showed the second man caked in mud, his hands pressed together in prayer, as rescuers brought him away on a stretcher. Rescuers called it a "miracle" after the disaster last week that has killed more than 1,300 people and left over 5,600 missing in Tibet and Nepal.

stories.title: Pat's v Bohs too close to call in FAI Cup quarter-final
stories.summary: Second and third place in the SSE Airtricity Men's Premier Division face off today in an exciting Club Orange FAI Cup quarter-final contest. Both teams have put up a fight to Shamrock Rovers, but with just a few games left, time may be running out for either team to win a miraculous league title. All eyes are on the cup. In the pick of the round, Bohemians make the short trip to Inchicore to face St Patrick's Athletic in Richmond Park, a trip that the Gypsies may have to get used to. Between the Bohs men’s and women’s teams there are seven games left in Dalymount Park in their respective leagues. The men also have a friendly against Bohemians Praha 1905, and their future is yet to be decided in the FAI Cup. After some farewell concerts, that will be it for the historic ground. Dalymount Park, as we know it, will be knocked down to make way for a brand new stadium. It was reported in June that Bohs were negotiating an agreement to play alongside their rivals Pat's for the next two seasons at least in Richmond Park.
